Situational Hook: Sapuka, 2045

Tahun 2045. Malam itu, Sapuka gelap. Angin barat bertiup kuat, ombak besar menghantam pantai, dan kapal yang membawa bahan bakar tertunda selama beberapa hari. Di sekolah, siswa kelas XII sedang mempersiapkan presentasi kelulusan, tetapi listrik padam. HP mereka hampir habis baterai. Internet tidak bisa digunakan dengan baik. Anak-anak kecil di rumah belajar menggunakan lampu kecil yang redup.

Di tengah kegelapan itu, seorang siswa bernama Arman menemukan sebuah kotak tua di ruang laboratorium sekolah. Di dalamnya terdapat gambar rancangan lama: “Sapuka Community Solar Project.” Ada sketsa panel surya di atap sekolah, turbin angin kecil di dekat pantai, dan baterai komunitas untuk menyimpan listrik.

“Can this old idea bring light back to Sapuka?”

Think First

  1. What happened to Sapuka in the story?
  2. Why did the island become dark?
  3. What did Arman find?
  4. Can students become problem solvers?
  5. How can renewable energy help a small island?
Kotak tua berisi rancangan panel surya, baterai, dan catatan proyek.

Learning Objectives

Setelah mempelajari chapter ini, peserta didik mampu:

  1. Memahami fungsi sosial Narrative Text untuk menghibur, menyampaikan konflik, dan menyampaikan nilai kehidupan.
  2. Mengidentifikasi struktur narrative: orientation → complication → sequence of events → resolution → reorientation/moral value.
  3. Menganalisis alur, konflik, tokoh, setting, dan pesan moral dalam cerita fiksi ilmiah sederhana.
  4. Menggunakan simple past tense, future expressions, descriptive language, dan dialogue sederhana.
  5. Menceritakan ulang satu adegan melalui storytelling pendek.
  6. Menulis narrative text bertema masa depan Sapuka dan energi terbarukan.
  7. Membuat storyboard/comic strip “My Island in the Future.”

MoT — Main Model Text

Orientation

The Last Light of Sapuka

In 2045, Sapuka was still a small island with a big heart. The sea was still blue, the people still helped each other, and the students still walked to school while the wind carried the smell of salt and seaweed. But life was not always easy. The weather changed more often than before. The west monsoon came with stronger winds, bigger waves, and longer boat delays.

One dark evening, the island lost its electricity. At first, people thought it would only last for one night. However, the boat that carried fuel from outside the island was delayed by rough seas. The waves were too high, and the harbor was not safe for the boat to arrive.

At SMA Negeri 6 Pangkajene dan Kepulauan, the Grade XII students were preparing their graduation presentation. They wanted to present their dreams for Sapuka’s future. But the classroom was dark. The projector did not work. Their phones had low battery. The internet connection was weak because many devices could not be charged.

Arman, a quiet student who liked repairing old radios and broken chargers, sat near the school laboratory. Nisa, his classmate, was drawing a future island map in her notebook. Fadil was trying to turn on a small emergency lamp, but the light was weak.

“This cannot continue,” Nisa said softly. “How can we talk about the future if we cannot even turn on the light?” Arman looked at the dark classroom. “Maybe the answer is already here,” he said.

Complication

Suddenly, the strong wind shook the laboratory window. A pile of old papers fell from a wooden shelf. Behind the papers, Arman saw a dusty metal box. On the top of the box, there was a faded label: Sapuka Community Solar Project — 2028.

Arman opened the box carefully. Inside, he found old drawings, simple circuit notes, a small solar panel, a broken sensor, and a plan for a community battery. There was also a sketch of the school roof with solar panels and a small wind turbine near the beach.

Nisa’s eyes became wide. “This is a renewable energy plan,” she said. Fadil looked unsure. “But this is old. Can it still work?” The next morning, Arman, Nisa, and Fadil showed the plan to Ms. Lina, their teacher. She explained that former students and teachers had dreamed that Sapuka could have cleaner energy, but the project had stopped because some tools were damaged and the school did not have enough support.

“Can we continue it?” Arman asked. Ms. Lina smiled. “You can try. But it will not be easy.” Some students laughed when they heard the idea. “You want to light the school with an old box?” one student said. For a moment, Arman felt embarrassed, but Nisa touched his shoulder. “A small idea can change the future,” she said. “Let’s try.”

Sequence of Events

The students started with what they had. Arman checked the old wires. Fadil cleaned the small solar panel. Nisa copied the design into a new notebook and drew a clearer future island map. Ms. Lina helped them make a list of tools: wires, small lamps, old batteries, tape, wood, and a simple switch.

After school, they asked villagers for help. A fisherman gave them old cables from a broken boat lamp. A seaweed farmer gave them wooden frames. A shop owner gave them a small used battery. Some younger students helped clean the study room. They did not have expensive technology. They only had patience, teamwork, and a strong reason.

Then, the weather became worse. One afternoon, strong wind damaged their wooden frame. The solar panel fell to the ground. Fadil looked at the broken frame and sighed. “We failed,” he said. Arman sat silently. His hands were dirty from dust and wire.

Nisa picked up the cracked wooden frame. “No. We learned one thing,” she said. “The frame was too weak. We can build a stronger one.” Ms. Lina nodded. “Every invention begins with mistakes.” The next day, the students improved their design. They moved the small solar panel to a safer place, used stronger wood, repaired the wires, and made an energy-saving schedule.

At sunset, they waited. The classroom was quiet. The sea was still rough outside. Children from nearby houses looked through the window. Arman pressed the switch. Nothing happened. Then, suddenly, a small lamp blinked once. Everyone held their breath. The lamp blinked again. Then it stayed on.

Resolution

“It works!” Nisa shouted. A small light filled the room. It was not very bright, but it was enough. Enough for students to read. Enough for a teacher to write on the board. Enough for one phone to charge. Enough to make people believe again.

That night, the school study room became the brightest place in the village. Children came with books. Grade XII students charged their phones only for learning and emergency messages. Ms. Lina helped the students prepare their graduation presentation under the small solar lamp.

The next week, the students presented their project in front of teachers, parents, and villagers. Nisa showed the future island map. Fadil explained how they repaired the wires. Arman explained how the solar panel and battery worked together. “We do not have a perfect system yet,” Arman said, “but we have started.”

Reorientation / Moral Value

Years later, people still remembered that small lamp. They called it the last light of Sapuka because it shone during one of the darkest nights. But for Arman, Nisa, Fadil, and their teacher, it was not the last light. It was the first light of a better future.

The story of Sapuka taught them that the future of an island does not depend only on big machines or outside help. It also depends on young people who care, teachers who guide, and communities that work together.

A small idea can change the future. Clean energy can bring hope. And Sapuka can shine again.

Model Text A — Very Easy to Easy

The Small Solar Lamp

Orientation

One evening in Sapuka, the wind blew softly from the sea. Lina, a Grade XII student, sat near the window of her house with an English book on her lap. The next day, she would have a speaking practice at school. She wanted to read her notes again, but suddenly the electricity went off. The room became dark. Outside, she could hear the sound of small waves and the voices of children calling each other in the street.

Complication

Lina looked at her phone. The battery was only three percent. Her younger brother, Rafi, also needed light to finish his homework. Their mother placed a small solar lamp on the table, but the lamp did not turn on. It was an old lamp that Lina’s father had bought years before.

“Maybe it is broken,” Rafi said.

Lina felt disappointed. She almost closed her book, but then she remembered Arman, her classmate, who liked repairing broken chargers and radios.

Sequence of Events

The next morning, Lina brought the solar lamp to school. During break time, she showed it to Arman and Nisa. Arman opened the lamp carefully. Nisa cleaned the small solar panel with a soft cloth. Inside the lamp, they found a loose wire.

“This wire is not connected,” Arman said. “We can try to repair it.”

They used tape, a small screwdriver, and an old wire from the laboratory. At first, the lamp still did not work. Lina felt nervous because she needed it that night. Then Nisa suggested putting the lamp under the sun for a few hours. They placed it near the classroom window where sunlight was strong.

Resolution

That night, Lina pressed the button again. For one second, nothing happened. Then the small lamp blinked. A warm yellow light filled the table. Rafi smiled and opened his notebook. Lina read her English notes aloud, and her mother sat beside them with a proud smile.

Moral Value

The lamp was small, but it brought light to their study time. Lina learned that renewable energy did not always begin with a big project. Sometimes, it began with a broken lamp, patient hands, and friends who wanted to help.

StructureContent
OrientationLina needs to study at night in Sapuka.
ComplicationThe electricity goes off and the solar lamp is broken.
EventsLina, Arman, and Nisa repair the lamp and charge it under sunlight.
ResolutionThe lamp turns on and helps Lina and Rafi study.
MoralSmall renewable energy tools can support learning.
Questions:
  1. Why did Lina need light at night?
  2. What problem did the solar lamp have?
  3. How did Lina’s friends help her?
Language Focus: Find three past verbs and one sentence with was or were.
Reflection: What small tool can help students study during a blackout?

Model Text B — Easy Level

The Wind Near the Harbor

Orientation

In 2045, Fadil often stood near Sapuka harbor after school. He liked watching the boats, the fishermen, and the sea birds flying above the water. During the west monsoon, the wind was very strong. It shook coconut trees, pushed waves against the rocks, and made people worry about boat schedules.

Most people saw the wind as a problem. Fadil saw it differently. He remembered a picture in his science book: a small wind turbine turning wind into electricity.

Complication

One afternoon, the electricity at school went off again. The Grade XII students were practicing their graduation presentation, but the projector could not turn on. Their teacher asked them to wait, but the room became hot and quiet. Fadil looked out of the window. The wind outside was strong enough to move the school flag quickly.

“The wind never stops,” Fadil whispered. “Maybe it can help us.”

Sequence of Events

After class, Fadil told Arman and Nisa about his idea. They wanted to build a small wind turbine model from recycled materials. Arman found a small motor from a broken toy. Nisa brought plastic pieces from used bottles. Fadil cut thin wooden sticks for the blades. Ms. Lina helped them read a simple diagram from an old energy book.

The first model looked good, but it did not move well. The blades were too heavy. Some students laughed and said, “It is only a toy.” Fadil felt embarrassed, but Arman said, “A model can teach us before we build something bigger.”

The next day, they made lighter blades. They placed the model near the harbor where the wind was steady. Slowly, the blades started to turn. The small motor made a tiny LED light blink.

Resolution

Fadil shouted happily. The light was very small, but the idea was big. He took the model back to school and showed it to his friends. This time, no one laughed. They understood that the same wind that delayed boats could also become useful energy.

Moral Value

The story teaches us to look at problems with new eyes. The wind can be a challenge, but with creativity, it can also become a source of hope.

StructureContent
OrientationFadil observes strong wind near Sapuka harbor.
ComplicationThe school loses electricity during graduation practice.
EventsStudents build and improve a small wind turbine model.
ResolutionThe model powers a small LED light.
MoralA challenge can become a solution.
Questions:
  1. What did Fadil often watch near the harbor?
  2. Why did the first model fail?
  3. What did the wind turbine model power?
Language Focus: Find two descriptive adjectives and two action verbs.
Reflection: What natural power around Sapuka can become useful?

Model Text C — Medium Level

A Battery for the Class

Orientation

One week before graduation, the Grade XII classroom was full of papers, drawings, and presentation notes. The students wanted to present a project called Clean Energy, Brighter Island. Nisa had drawn a future island map. Arman had prepared a simple explanation about solar panels. Fadil had collected photos of the school and the harbor.

They had one problem. Their small solar panel worked only during the day. At night, when they had time to practice after helping their families, the classroom was dark.

Complication

“We collect sunlight in the morning,” Nisa said, “but we lose it at night. How can we save the energy for later?”

The class became silent. They had talked about solar energy many times, but they had never thought seriously about storage. Without a battery, the panel could not help them after sunset.

Sequence of Events

Arman remembered an old black battery in the school storage room. It was dusty, weak, and almost forgotten. Fadil carried it carefully to the classroom. Ms. Lina reminded them, “Be careful. A battery is useful, but it must be handled safely.”

They cleaned the battery, checked the cables, and connected it to the small solar panel. The first test failed. The lamp turned on for only five minutes, then died. Fadil sighed. “It is too weak.”

Nisa looked at the notebook. “Maybe the battery is not the only problem. Maybe we are using too much energy at once.”

They changed their plan. They used only one small LED lamp. They charged only one phone for emergency messages. They made an energy-saving schedule: study first, charging later, no unnecessary lights.

Resolution

That night, the lamp stayed on for almost two hours. The students practiced their presentation under the small but steady light. They did not waste the energy. They used it carefully, and it was enough.

Moral Value

The story teaches us that technology needs responsibility. Renewable energy is powerful, but it becomes more useful when people learn to save, share, and use it wisely.

StructureContent
OrientationStudents prepare a clean energy presentation.
ComplicationThe solar panel cannot help them at night without storage.
EventsThey test an old battery, fail, and create an energy-saving schedule.
ResolutionThe lamp stays on long enough for practice.
MoralEnergy must be stored and used wisely.
Questions:
  1. Why did the students need a battery?
  2. Why did the first test fail?
  3. What rule did the students make for using energy?
Language Focus: Find one sentence with could or would, and three past verbs.
Reflection: Why is saving energy as important as producing energy?

Model Text D — Local Context

When the Boat Did Not Come

Orientation

During the west monsoon, the sea around Sapuka often became rough. The waves turned white, the wind pushed against the houses, and people checked the harbor many times a day. One week, the boat that carried fuel did not come. At first, the villagers waited calmly. They were used to delays. But on the fourth night, the electricity became unstable.

Complication

At school, the problem became serious. Grade XII students needed to prepare for exams and graduation. Teachers could not print materials. Some students could not charge their phones for learning. Younger children tried to read near small lamps at home. Everyone waited for the boat, but the sea was still too rough.

Arman looked at the dark classroom and remembered something behind the laboratory: an old solar panel covered with dust.

Sequence of Events

The next morning, Arman invited Nisa and Fadil to check the panel. It was dirty, but not completely broken. Nisa cleaned it slowly. Fadil looked for wires. Arman asked Ms. Lina if they could use an old battery from the storage room.

Some students were doubtful. “That panel is too small,” one of them said. “It cannot help the island.”

Arman answered quietly, “Maybe it cannot help the whole island today. But it can help one room tonight.”

After school, they asked villagers for support. A fisherman gave old cables from a broken boat lamp. A seaweed farmer gave wooden frames. A shop owner gave a small switch. The project became a community effort. People did not bring expensive machines. They brought what they had.

The first night, the system failed. The wire became loose, and the lamp turned off. The second night, the battery worked for only a short time. On the third night, after many small repairs, the lamp stayed on long enough for children to read.

Resolution

When the fuel boat finally arrived, the villagers were relieved. But they had already learned something important. Waiting for fuel was not the only answer. Sapuka also needed cleaner and more independent energy sources.

Moral Value

A crisis can open a new idea. The story teaches us that small islands need courage, cooperation, and local solutions. Sapuka’s future can be brighter when students, teachers, and villagers work together.

StructureContent
OrientationThe fuel boat is delayed during the west monsoon.
ComplicationSchool and home learning are affected by unstable electricity.
EventsStudents and villagers repair an old solar panel system.
ResolutionThe lamp helps students read before the fuel boat arrives.
MoralCrisis can inspire local solutions.
Questions:
  1. Why did the boat not come?
  2. What problem happened at school?
  3. How did the villagers help the students?
Language Focus: Find one dialogue sentence and two time connectors.
Reflection: What can Sapuka learn from boat delays?

Model Text E — Student-Like Model

My Island in 2045

Orientation

In 2045, my island looked familiar but brighter. Sapuka still had blue sea, small boats, seaweed ropes, coconut trees, and people who greeted each other on the road. But the school roof was covered with solar panels. Near the harbor, a small wind turbine turned slowly. At night, solar lamps lit the path from the school to the houses.

I was a Grade XII student, and my class had one important job: to protect the community battery. The battery stored energy from the school panels and helped the study room stay bright at night.

Complication

One night, a strong storm came from the west. The wind was loud, and the sea was rough. Rain hit the windows like small stones. Suddenly, some lights in the village went off. Children came to the school study room because it was the safest bright place near their homes.

Then the energy board showed a warning: Battery Low.

Sequence of Events

Everyone looked worried. Some students wanted to charge all their phones at once. Others wanted to turn on more lights. Our teacher stopped us.

“Energy is hope,” she said, “but hope must be shared wisely.”

My friends and I made a quick plan. First, we turned off unused lamps. Second, we allowed only one phone for emergency messages. Third, we asked children to sit together under two study lamps. Fourth, we wrote the storm updates on the board so people did not need to check their phones again and again.

After the storm, we checked the solar panels. Leaves and saltwater covered some parts. We cleaned them together. A few villagers repaired the frame near the roof. By afternoon, the panels started collecting sunlight again.

Resolution

That night, the study room became bright again. The children read their books, parents smiled outside the room, and our teacher said that the battery had survived because we used energy wisely.

Moral Value

My island in 2045 was not perfect. Storms still came, and problems still appeared. But Sapuka was ready because people worked together. The future was not only about technology. It was about responsibility, care, and the courage to protect our island.

StructureContent
OrientationSapuka in 2045 has solar panels, wind turbine, and community battery.
ComplicationA storm causes lights to go off and battery becomes low.
EventsStudents manage energy wisely and clean panels after the storm.
ResolutionThe study room becomes bright again.
MoralA better future needs technology and responsibility.
Questions:
  1. What renewable energy tools existed in Sapuka 2045?
  2. Why did the battery become important during the storm?
  3. How did the students save energy?
Language Focus: Find two future setting phrases and two descriptive adjectives.
Reflection: What do you want Sapuka to have in 2045?

Listening Section — The Night Sapuka Went Dark

Storytelling Script

Narrator: It was the year 2045. The night in Sapuka was darker than usual. The west wind was strong, and the sea was rough. The boat that carried fuel did not come because the waves were too high.

Fadil: My phone battery is only five percent. The projector is dead. How can we practice?

Nisa: The classroom is too dark. We need light.

Arman: Wait. Maybe there is an emergency lamp in the laboratory.

Narrator: Arman took a flashlight and walked to the old laboratory. Nisa and Fadil followed him. Suddenly, a pile of old papers fell from a shelf.

Nisa: Arman, look! There is a box behind the papers.

Arman: It says… “Sapuka Community Solar Project.”

Ms. Lina: Every bright future begins with one brave step.

Listening setting: siswa belajar dengan lampu kecil setelah proyek berhasil.

Listening Activities

  1. Choose the correct answer: When did the story happen? Why did the fuel boat not come?
  2. Put the events in order: electricity went off → students went to laboratory → Arman opened box → Ms. Lina explained.
  3. Complete the words: The west wind was ____. The sea was ____.
  4. Identify feelings: Fadil = worried, Arman = curious, Ms. Lina = supportive.
  5. Predict what will happen next.

A. Finding the Old Design

Arman: Nisa, look at this box.
Nisa: What is it?
Arman: It says “Sapuka Community Solar Project.”
Nisa: Open it carefully.
Arman: Solar panels on the school roof!
Nisa: I am not sure, but we can try.

B. Asking the Teacher

Fadil: Ma’am, can this project work?
Ms. Lina: Maybe. It will not be easy, but you can start with a small lamp.
Arman: Will you help us?
Ms. Lina: Of course. Every big change begins with a small step.

C. Convincing Villagers

Villager: Can students do that?
Nisa: We are starting small.
Villager: I have old cables. You can use them.

JCoT — Joint Construction of the Text

Topic: The Solar Lamp for Our Classroom

PartPlanning Notes
OrientationOne evening in Sapuka, the Grade XII students stayed at school.
ComplicationThe electricity went off; students could not study.
Event 1Arman found a broken solar lamp.
Event 2Nisa cleaned the panel and Fadil repaired the wire.
Event 3The teacher helped them test the lamp.
ResolutionThe lamp turned on; students studied together.
MoralSmall renewable energy tools can support learning.

Shared Writing Example

One evening in Sapuka, the Grade XII students stayed at school to study for an English exam. The sky was dark, and the wind was strong. Suddenly, the electricity went off. The classroom became silent.

Arman remembered an old solar lamp in the school storage room. He took a flashlight and went there with Nisa and Fadil. The lamp was dusty, and the wire was loose. Nisa cleaned the small solar panel. Fadil repaired the wire carefully. Arman checked the battery. Their teacher helped them test the lamp safely.

At first, nothing happened. Then, the lamp blinked. A few seconds later, it turned on. The students smiled. The light was not very strong, but it was enough for reading. The story teaches us that hope can come from simple things. A small lamp can bring light, and teamwork can bring a better future.
